1940461,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.9.1.1.2,1958-06-03,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,STATEMENT ON POLITICAL,DEVELOPMENTS,Mr. Speaker, on May 27 the

Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) asked whether the house could be given any report on the developments in France. At that time I indicated that in view of the situation then prevailing it might be well to postpone any statement.

In recent weeks Canadians have watched the French political scene with concern and sympathy. Considering how closely our history and traditions are interwoven with those of France, the deep interest taken by our people in recent events there is not surprising. We now welcome the solution of the parliamentary crisis in France and express the sincere hope that under the leadership of their wartime hero, General Charles de Gaulle, as prime minister, France will enjoy political stability and economic prosperity.

I know that I speak for all Canadians when I say I am confident that the warm and friendly relations which are inherent as between Canada and France, and which have been strengthened in two world wars and in recent years by our common membership in NATO, will continue as before.

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL

Lionel Chevrier (Laurier):,Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,LABOUR CONDITIONS,NON-OPERATING RAILWAY UNIONS-STATUS OF CONCILIATION PROCEEDINGS,May I direct a question to the Minister of Labour, or alternatively in his absence to the Minister of Transport. My question is based upon a press statement in a Montreal newspaper of recent date entitled "" Last Bid in Rail Dispute"", and it points to the seriousness of the situation as it was then, only a few days ago. I read but one paragraph, which is as follows:

The odds are stacked heavily against averting a deadlock over union wage and welfare demands involving more than $100,000,000 a year for the railways. Collapse of the public conciliation proceedings is seen by labour observers who forecast another serious railway-union crisis close on the heels of the three-day strike of diesel firemen against the Canadian Pacific Railway earlier this month.
What is the government doing to avert a strike between non-operating employees of the railways and the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company?

,Liberal,,Lionel Chevrier,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=e2b15c2f-35a6-4e4e-8e52-a4357fdebc0d&Language=E&Section=ALL

1940471,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.9.3.1.2,1958-06-03,0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32,ca.m.6630,Mr. Hazen Argue (Assiniboia):,,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,ATOMIC ENERGY,PROPOSED STUDY OF CONTROL OF NUCLEAR TESTS,I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Would the Prime Minister care to comment on the report in this morning's press that President Eisenhower has approved a message to Soviet Premier Khrushchev indicating his readiness to have Polish, Czech and other scientists included in proposed scientific talks on how to police a suspension of nuclear weapons tests?
Can the Prime Minister say whether Canada will be included in such scientific talks, and whether Canada has been consulted in this regard?

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Hazen Robert Argue,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32&Language=E&Section=ALL
1940472,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.9.3.1.3,1958-06-03,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,ATOMIC ENERGY,PROPOSED STUDY OF CONTROL OF NUCLEAR TESTS,Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman was kind enough to give me notice of his question. As I said yesterday in my remarks about Mr. Khrushchev's letter to me, I
welcome the Soviet readiness to participate in a study of the technicalities of the controls required to accompany a suspension of nuclear tests.

In his letter of May 30 to President Eisenhower, Mr. Khrushchev was somewhat more specific about the arrangements for the meeting of experts and made a number of suggestions concerning the time, place and duration of the meeting, as well as about the participants. It is a matter of satisfaction to me that President Eisenhower has indicated that for his part he does not wish to allow questions of this kind to impede the early convening of a meeting of the experts.

Canada has for some time been in consultation with the United States, the United Kingdom and with others of the North Atlantic treaty alliance on this question. We had the opportunity of examining in advance and consulting upon the draft of the letter sent by the President on May 24, and we made our views known to the United States department of state. The particular statement which was reported in this morning's press was not the subject of specific consultations. However, we had in an earlier communication to Washington referred to the possibility that the Soviet union might wish to include representatives from other communist countries and we had made no obj ections.

With regard to Canadian participation in the talks, I would recall that President Eisenhower's letter of May 24 referred to the inclusion of scientists from the United Kingdom and France and ""other countries having experts who are advanced in knowledge of how to detect nuclear tests"". I think I can safely observe that not many countries are better equipped than Canada to make such a contribution, and in the event of Canada receiving a request to provide an expert or a team of experts, we will certainly agree to do so.

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL

Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister,NATIONAL DEFENCE,NUCLEAR WEAPONS,TRANSPORTATION BY AIR- CRAFT ACROSS CANADA,Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition indicated in general terms his intention to ask whether the charges that strategic air command bombers fly over Canada with nuclear weapons in the direction of the Soviet union are true.

First of all, I should state that the letter from Mr. Khrushchev is still being studied, and I would not wish to take a definitive position now upon any of its details. May I, however, draw the attention of the Leader of the Opposition to page 3123 of Hansard for January 10, when the matter was before the

Inquiries of the Ministry house, and also page 3188 of Hansard of January 11, where earlier remarks by the Minister of National Defence and myself are to be found. Those replies and the answer given by the Minister of National Defence on November 27, 1957, at page 1566 of Hansard provide much of the answer to the present question. I refer specifically now to the . latter question which appears at page 1566, where the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) asked this question:

May I direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. In view of a reported statement made by the British foreign minister to the effect that United States bombers flying on routine flights over Britain carry live bombs in order to maintain a state of readiness at all times, can the minister state whether United States planes with such bombs are permitted to fly over Canada?
To which the Minister of National Defence replied as follows:
By agreement with the United States, only with prior permission from Canada.

In the passages to which I have referred the house was informed that United States-bomber aircraft carry nuclear weapons over Canada only with prior permission from Canada; that each flight is dealt with separately by specific application, and there is no blanket authority; that the weapons are inactivated in order to avoid the possibility of accidents; and that the procedures being followed are unchanged from those which had been instituted by the previous government.

The earlier questions were more concerned with the nature of the international arrangements and with safety precautions than with the fact that flights by the strategic air command might be taking place over Canada. Nevertheless, the answers to which I have referred did make it plain that such flights do take place. The Leader of the Opposition, I am sure, will at once recognize that it would not be in the public interest for me to give any indication of either the frequency of such flights or the numbers of aircraft involved. However, in order to provide information such as that to those who are of the privy council the government will at all times be prepared to give that information privately. However, 1 wish to make one thing perfectly clear, that none of those flights to which I have made reference has approached or been to the borders of Canada and the U.S.S.R.

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL

1940545,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.22.2,1958-06-03,3c7abf33-5a24-4c46-87e9-5a6c9d457af5,ca.m.9967,Mr. Alexis Caron (Hull):,,DOMINION-PROVINCIAL FISCAL RELATIONS,,,Mr. Speaker, when the unrelenting clock stopped my remarks last night, I was speaking about the unemployment situation. I should now like to quote the very figures given by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), who said that on April 30 there were more than 722,000 unemployed in Canada. It is an alarming situation considering that never, at any time, since the depression of 1930-1935, has the April unemployment figure been so large in this country. And any time unemployment is up for discussion, everybody tries to pass the buck.

Whatever might be the cause of unemployment, whatever the views of this or that man on the subject, and whatever the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) might have said about it during the recent elections or those of last June 10-whatever each man's private opinion may be in the matter- the incontrovertible fact stands out that the number of unemployed in this country has

never been higher. This is a danger, a hazard even for public peace because we must not forget, as Saint Thomas says, that: ""To be virtuous, people must have a modicum of comfort"". And if a considerable number of our labouring fellow-citizens are practically starving, there is always a danger that they will rise against the state, the municipalities or the provinces. Therefore it is time that our government give its full attention to extending a helpful hand to the unemployed.

I said, not more than a few days ago, that in the Hull area alone, 51.8 per cent of the unemployed are people willing to work but unable to do so because there is no work to be had. They want help because they are not getting unemployment insurance, have used up all their stamps and are no longer qualified for benefits. They are human beings in need of help and it is up to the municipality to do what it can to feed them. The welfare services are doing their share, but things are now so bad that people are even asking that their rent be taken care of, so as to avoid being turned into the streets. Something must be done without fail.

As I said a moment ago, whatever responsibility might rest elsewhere, this government must face its own responsibility. I am referring to the situation which prevailed in 1953-1954 when the provincial government was paying 50 per cent of public relief. That year, the city of Hull spent $90,000 out of a total of $180,000 on relief. In this year 1957-1958, when cities have only 25 per cent to pay as their share, so far the city of Hull has had to spend $115,000 which represents a total of more than $480,000 for public assistance. Can it continue to provide all that is required when the unemployment situation is not the responsibility of the municipalities? In fact, the responsibility lies with those governments which lacked foresight and, in my opinion, it lies mostly with the present government which allowed us to lose our markets at a time when Canada with a population of only 17 million is producing for a population of over 48 million people. Accordingly, those surpluses have to be marketed abroad, and when Canada loses those markets, it means unemployment, plant shutdowns and evictions.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the present government, because it is responsible for this problem, to give the municipalities a chance to undertake at once public works for the immediate relief of the unemployed.
Speaking of public works, may I mention that for years we have been asking for a bridge between Ottawa and Hull. While such a bridge is recognized as a necessity, succes-
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations sive governments have claimed that it should be paid for on a 33J per cent basis by each level of government.

Well, Mr. Speaker, that situation is growing worse day by day. It might be necessary for the present government to build it entirely at its own expense. If anyone wishes to know how much it would cost, I would quote a figure mentioned by the Prime Minister when he was visiting Hull; he said at the time that the bridge would probably cost about $12 million. Well, if $12 million have to be spent in three years to relieve the serious unemployment problem, I think the present government should assume the entire cost, because I am convinced that if we wait for Quebec to pay its share of one third, we shall never have it, because that government is concerned not with the welfare of people but with petty politics only. And because the people of Hull elected a Liberal member to the provincial legislature, we can be sure of not getting any help, especially in the light of the statement made by the premier of Quebec in Shawinigan Falls, when he said: ""You will have no bridge if you don't elect a member of the Union Nationale.""

Mr. Speaker, we cannot wait indefinitely. I would therefore ask the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) to make an earnest study of that situation in order that the building of that bridge may begin in the very near future.

Mr. Speaker, I could go on and refer to a lot of public works which are urgent in my riding; and perhaps I could also, under the circumstances, answer many statements which were made on both sides of the house. However, I conclude by asking the members of the Union Nationale wing in the Conservative party to make their stand very clear.

How do they stand in the matter of the sharing of tax rights as between the government of Ottawa and that of Quebec? I hope that they are not going to keep talking about confederation and all the rest of it, but that they will tell us intelligently and frankly what is going to be their attitude when the government they are supporting will simply continue the policy of the preceding governments. Then we might be able to believe in their sincerity if they agree that their slogan of the last election: ""Canada gives to foreigners but the province gives to its own citizens"", is not true.

We would also like to know their stand in the matter of our contributions to the Colombo plan. We also want to know, now that they sit in Ottawa, whether they have enlarged their horizon and intend to live like Canadians, or narrow-minded Quebecers who want to stay in their reserve for the rest of their lives.

1940546,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.22.3,1958-06-03,4f4d70a2-4448-4652-bf73-422decd108d3,ca.m.1470,Mr. Noel Dorion (Bellechasse):,,DOMINION-PROVINCIAL FISCAL RELATIONS,,,Mr. Speaker, as a newcomer to the house, I had no intention of taking part in this debate. However, because of certain allegations made by some of our hon. friends opposite, and because of the rather light-hearted way in which they have been dealing with matters of principle, I did feel it would be proper that one voice at least from the province of Quebec be raised in rebuttal. In speaking then as a member for that province, I feel that I will be at the same time expressing feelings of a sound Canadianism.

In fact, it is from that rather general angle of Canadianism, that I propose to deal with one of the two problems referred to in the non confidence motion put by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). The amendment comprises two distinct parts. The first deals with the recession and with the difficulties that it might involve for the municipalities and towns of this country. The second deals with the equalization principle and consequently touches upon one of the fundamental problems which are of interest to the people as a whole. It is with this second paragraph of the amendment put by the Leader of the Opposition that I should like to deal briefly today and to define exactly the views of the Conservative members from the province of Quebec, explaining also why the people of that province voted Conservative during the* last elections and expressed its confidence in the present Prime Minister of this country (Mr. Diefenbaker).

Mr. Speaker, there is nothing more solid, nor indeed more indispensable, than the legal foundations on which any doctrine must rest whose general acceptance is necessary to the welfare of the provinces and of the country as a whole.

I shall take the liberty-and I apologize for mentioning certain things that will seem elementary to most of the hon. members in this house-but in support of my arguments, I shall take the liberty to bring up certain sections of the constitution which too often seemed to have been overlooked, certain sections of the constitution, which are treasured in the province of Quebec, because we feel that respect for such sections is one of the essential conditions for the survival of the racial group which the province of Quebec has the duty to protect and to safeguard.

Section 118 of the British North America Act provides in fact that subsidies will be granted by the federal government to the various provinces. As everybody knows, that section was amended in 1907, and the amendment was adopted not only by the federal government, but also by imperial statute as had been the case for the Act of 1867.

In other words, the procedure adopted clearly showed that a constitutional problem was involved since recourse was being had to the imperial authorities that in 1867 had sanctioned in substance the agreement between the provinces which had led to confederation. Does this mean, Mr. Speaker, that by section 118 of the constitution, the principle of subsidies being paid to provinces was being recognized as a general rule? My answer is no. I remember reading a speech made in this house by the hon. member for Montmagny-l'Islet (Mr. Lesage) in which he seemed to recognize the ratification of the principle of subsidies to the provinces whereas, when referring to the debates, and in particular to those of the Quebec conference, we realize that members of the constituent assembly had refused to lay down as a principle this method of financing provinces. And it is so true-and I hope my learned friends in the opposition will not hold it against me if I quote one jurist who is active in their ranks-that Mr. Louis-Philippe Pigeon, who was legal adviser to the hon. Adelard Godbout about the years 1940 to 1945, dealing with this very problem, recalled that, according to Pope's Confederation Documents containing summaries of the debates of the various conferences that led to the confederation agreement, this principle had been rejected. Indeed here is, according to the Quebec Bar Association Review, volume 3, 1943, how Mr. Pigeon understood this rejection:

Now, is it known that the granting of subsidies to provinces was one of the listed powers of the federal government, in the draft submitted to the Quebec conference and that it was struck off in the course of the discussion?

In other words, the constituent provinces of 1867 did not wish, in creating the federal state, to become its vassals. That is why we cannot condone too frequent infringements on basic provincial rights. Moreover, that is what, on many occasions, led the province of Quebec to express its formal determination to stick to the constitution which governs us.

Mr. Speaker, I am not one to claim that the provinces have an exclusive power in the field of direct taxation. In the early days of this session, I heard the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) refer to those who claim for the provinces the exclusive right to direct taxation.

I have much respect and admiration for the hon. member for Laurier, and I presume that he must be in possession of accurate information on which to base his statement to the effect that such theories are accepted and advocated in the province of Quebec. As for me-and by the way I do not know any members from the province of Quebec

who felt in coming here that their thoughts and ideas were regimented-I positively state that we came here freely and loyally because we truly believe that we belong to a party offering all possible guarantees that the spirit and the letter of our constitution will be kept inviolate.

I readily recognize that under the act by which we are governed since 1867, as far as direct taxation and direct contributions are concerned, there is concurrent jurisdiction. But this concurrence of rights and powers is not an ordinary one: it calls for certain precise details and distinctions.
I heard my good friend from Hull (Mr. Caron) pour forth his ideas in bulk. This is surely not the proper way to deal with a question as momentous as the subject matter of this debate.

To show those necessary distinctions and differences, with the permission of the house, we shall now have a look at the two sections dealing with the distribution of power between the federal and provincial governments, sections 92 and 91 of the constitution. What does section 92 say? Let us point out first of all that the preamble is just as important, just as essential as the section proper. Let us therefore read subsection 2 of section 92 with its preamble:
92. In each province, the Legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects hereinafter enumerated:
And subsection 2 provides:

column2: Direct taxation within the province in order to the raising of a revenue for provincial purposes.

column1: In other words, section 92 reserves to the provinces an exclusive right of raising direct taxes, provided this right is exercized within the limits of provincial jurisdiction for specifically provincial purposes.

Against this let us now read what power the members of the constituent assembly conferred upon the federal government. This is found in section 91, subsection 1, paragraph 3 and, reading only paragraph 3, this is what we find:

column2: The raising of money by any mode or system of taxation.

column1: This is a power belonging to the federal government. Of course, on the basis of those words lifted out of their context, it may be thought that an absolute power is granted the federal government. But that is not the way to interpret a text. Surely I could not tell my learned friends in the opposition, among whom there are brilliant lawyers, the rules of interpretation. To have its full

Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations meaning, a text must necessarily be read within its context. What does section 91 contain when read according to this rule? First of all, here are the provisions of its preamble:

91. It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces.

Now, as we have just seen, among the subjects assigned exclusively to the provinces by the lawmakers, is that of direct taxation for provincial purposes. Consequently any federal government which levies direct taxation for provincial purposes conforms neither to the letter nor to the spirit of the constitution. So true is this that it has been so determined by the privy council itself.

May I be allowed, at this juncture, to refer to a case often cited before the courts, i.e., ""Bank of Toronto vs Lambe, 1887"". In this instance, one of the Lords of Her Majesty's privy council-Lord Atkin,
I believe-expressed himself as follows: (Text):
This very conflict between the two sections was noticed by way of illustration in the case of Parsons.
(Translation):
This Parson case is very often cited in constitutional cases.
(Text):

So 'the raising of money by any mode or system of taxation' is enumerated among the classes of subjects in sect. 91; but, though the description is sufficiently large and general to include 'direct taxation within the province, in order to the raising of a revenue for provincial purposes,' assigned to the provincial legislatures by sect. 92, it obviously could not have been intended that, in this instance also, the general power should override the particular one."" Their Lordships adhere to that view, and hold that, as regards direct taxation within the province to raise revenue for provincial purposes, that subject falls wholly within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures.
(Translation):

I have no wish to bore you with quotations. However, there is another highly important and well known case which has been made law. The case was argued before the privy council under the Liberal administration under Mr. Mackenzie King. The point of issue was social legislation adopted by the Bennett government. I might be wrong, but I seem to remember that the federal government's case was put by the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. Their lordships had declared at that time that certain social security laws were ultra vires. The judgment handed down reproduces almost verbatim the terms of the decision to which I

Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations have just referred. In this connection, may I quote an opinion given by an eminent member of the Quebec bench, a gentleman who sat on the highest court in the land and who has, in fact, left a work of lasting merit, from which the province of Quebec and this country as a whole are much the gainers. Here is what Hon. Justice P. B. Migneault wrote in the Revue du Droit, 19371938, with regard to this highly important matter.

It must also be noted that there Is no justification for giving to federal powers mentioned in general terms an extension such that a similar provincial power, expressly mentioned, would remain devoid of useful application. Thus parliament can collect revenues by any method or system of taxation, and the provincial legislature is authorized to levy direct taxes within the limits of the province, as revenue for the discharge of provincial obligations. Obviously, the general terms of the federal power must be restricted to leave room for the provincial attribution.

Well, Mr. Speaker, that is, in my opinion, the doctrine implemented by the constituent provinces, under articles 91 and 92; that is the doctrine which has always been recognized up to recently, the doctrine confirmed by a decision of the privy council, confirmed by the greatest jurist we ever had in French Canada, Hon. Justice Migneault, and also by none other than the legal adviser of the Hon. Adelard Godbout who, as far back as 1940, when he was prime minister of the province of Quebec, laid it aside.

What happened afterwards? Until 1917, that doctrine has remained unchallenged for the excellent reason that the federal government, in spite of its power under the constitution, in spite of the recognition of its right to collect taxes by any means of taxation, has scrupulously respected the equal rights of the provinces. And it needed that catas-trophy of war, which cost Canada its best blood for the protection of its rights and institutions, to muster as it were all its sources of revenues so as to bring to a successful conclusion the mission to which Canada had dedicated herself.
It was Sir Thomas White who, in 1917, first introduced personal income tax. It was>

the right of the federal government but such a right had never been exercised since confederation. Yet Sir Thomas White was careful to state that it would be for the duration of the difficult period which Canada was going through at the time.

Since that time, we have had a succession of governments. The first were Liberal governments but, instead of keeping the promise made, they preferred to cling to that tax which today remains in our statutes and which we are still paying.

I do not deny that in so doing the federal government is exercising a right, but I do point out that up to 1917 this right had been exercised only by the provinces which, for that matter, had made a moderate use of it. Consequently, when today provinces avail themselves of a right which, for the past 40 or 50 years the federal government had not exercised in spite of its power to do so, I say it is wrong to assert that this is promoting national disunity. The promoters of national disunity are those who refuse to recognize the rights and powers of the provinces.

If you want to prosecute the war on a basis of co-operation with the provinces we are prepared to co-operate; but if the prime minister insists that everything has to be predicated upon the principle of a report to which we object, then there is no alternative open to my colleagues and to myself but to withdraw and to leave these wreckers of confederation, under the guise of patriotism, to continue to carry on their nefarious work.

During that period, in surrendering its sources of income, Quebec contributed $2,258,381,000 to the federal treasury, while on the other hand, because of its faithfulness toward that party we have dislodged in the last election, it received $102,930,272.80. I mention those 80 cents because of course, they have to be taken into consideration in such a pittance.

What I want to stress in all this is the fact that in entering into an agreement the federal government was recognizing the existence of the provincial taxation power. One does not enter into an agreement when one can grasp everything with impunity. A thief does not enter into any agreement with his victim. But in this case an agreement was entered into which, I repeat, expressly recognized the principle of provincial taxation power. But, Mr. Speaker, I have always understood- and this seems to me an elementary tenet of law-that an agreement implies the free and willing consent of the parties. An agreement entered into with a knife held to one's throat is no agreement. When a robber walks into a bank, brandishes a gun and tells the cashier: ""Give me all the money you've got in the till"", and is handed the money, this is surely no agreement. An agreement implies the free and willing consent of the parties, and if they are not at liberty to accept the terms, this is no agreement but oppression or dictatorship. Well, that is what was seen at some of the conferences held between the provinces and the federal government of the time.
I shall but briefly mention the conferences which took place at intervals until 1945, to come to the meeting that has been called the conference on re-establishment.
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations

The reports of the time make interesting reading. They indicate that the province which appeared to be going into isolation was not Quebec, but rather Ontario. Why was it acting this way? Simply-and with good reason-because it held this federal action to be contrary to the letter and the spirit of confederation.

In 1946 the 1945 conference was resumed. This time it was a Liberal premier, Mr. Macdonald, of Nova Scotia, who opposed that form of forced agreement and who denounced the intrusion of the federal government into fields outside its jurisdiction. I do not know that there were any among our eminent colleagues, now in opposition, who at that time raised an outcry against that particular provincial premier, who was forced to accept the conditions which the then federal minister of finance attempted to impose upon the provinces. Had this gentleman been premier of Quebec, would he have been greeted differently? There is one thing which is not generally known, and it is this: in the province of Quebec a system of purges was applied throughout the ranks of the Liberal party. I had heard of such things happening in other countries. We have been told, for instance, that in certain countries behind the iron curtain, whenever an active party member is so unfortunate as to deviate in fact and in conscience from the party line, he is purged forthwith. Such things occasionally happen in the province of Quebec. Certain Liberals are purged. Some members of the party have been cast into outer darkness, in spite of the fact that they had made an outstanding contribution to their group. Let there be no misgivings on this score. I am not referring to the Liberals who are sitting here, but rather to some of their Quebec friends. That is the kind of broad-mindedness of which, alas! we have had certain samples right here. The hon. members who provided the samples were surely not endeavouring to safeguard national unity; rather were they attempting to sow dissension among us, to the prejudice of that union which is characteristic of the Conservative party and is at the source of its greatness and appeal.

Mr. Speaker, those first agreements were followed by others. Save for Ontario and Quebec, who refrained on matters of principle, all the other provinces have had to sign. Newfoundland did likewise, when it, in turn, entered confederation. Newfoundland's union with Canada was a memorable event,

and even if its only benefit had been to bring among us the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), I would be very happy about it because I have the greatest respect and consideration for him.

Lionel Chevrier (Laurier):,Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader,DOMINION-PROVINCIAL FISCAL RELATIONS,,,Mr. Speaker, I hope the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) will excuse me if I do not at this time follow him in the very able, judicial and legal argument which he has put before the house. 1940569,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.22.26,1958-06-03,c17c9546-ec4f-47a5-95a7-27b20ceb25f5,ca.m.1993,Mr. Balcer:,Solicitor General of Canada,DOMINION-PROVINCIAL FISCAL RELATIONS,,,And a political one, yes. I want to tell him that the proposals of the federal government are not yet known, but I am convinced that they will be made on a very different basis from those of the former government.

It is quite clear that they were not made on a different basis. They were made on exactly the same basis, but increased, and I do not know that the hon. gentleman intervened in this debate to point out what his position is. So that as we stand now, we have a complete contradiction between what the government has done and what one of its ministers has said.

With the permission of the house I should now like to take a look at the attitude of the premier of the province of Ontario. At a federal-provincial meeting held on March 9, 1956, Premier Frost is reported to have said that he was definitely against the present basis of equalization payments because it was unsatisfactory to the province of Ontario and too generous to the other provinces. He made the suggestion that the average per capita yield of the standard tax rates in the two highest yield provinces-which in effect is the present basis-should be changed and he proposed that the top four provinces or even the national average should be used to determine these payments. He is reported to have gone even a step further and to have stated that the present formula was too generous to the province of Quebec.

Here, in order that there may be no misunderstanding about what I say, I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of March 10, 1956, outlining the views of the premier of the province of Ontario at that time. 1 quote from the article as follows:
Mr. Frost said the unfairness to Ontario of the present formula can be demonstrated by comparisons with certain of the other provinces, notably Quebec and Alberta.
I take our sister province of Quebec because with her we are most closely associated. Economically speaking, we are most alike and with her we have many things in common.""

Like Ontario, the premier said. Quebec is rapidly growing and expanding and has large concentration of manufacturing industries and population. Under the federal formula Quebec will have the allowance of the standard rates which are proposed and an annual adjustment grant of more than $40 million.
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations

Mr. Frost said he had no doubt Quebec needs this additional money and could put it to good use, but if this is the federal assessment of Quebec's need, how much greater it should be for Ontario in the light of this province's larger population and industrial structure and all of the costs which accompany industrial development?

I do not in the slightest blame the premier of Ontario for taking that attitude. After all, he is defending the interests of the taxpayers of his province. But just let us for a moment take a look at his thesis and compare it with that of the present government. According to Mr. Frost, Quebec and Ontario are competing against each other to attract new industries and that is a fact because there are in both provinces Large concentrations of industrial development. There are in both provinces tremendous amounts of water power, although those in the province of Quebec I believe are greater. Quebec would have an advantage over Ontario because the over-all level of wages is lower. On the other hand, Ontario at present would have an advantage over Quebec because taxes are lower there than they are in the province of Quebec. However, if the present basis of equalization is used, Quebec receives a high equalization payment of the order of $40 million or more per year. This payment, according to Mr. Frost, would place Quebec in a position of lowering its taxes, thus acquiring an additional advantage over Ontario as far as the location of new industries are concerned.

I hope I am not being misunderstood in what I say because I am sure no one would quarrel with the premier of the province of Ontario for approaching the problem from this angle. That is why he felt that, because of the formula that is advanced by the federal government, it was too generous to certain provinces, particularly the provinces of Quebec and Alberta, as I stated a moment ago. Thus, while the Prime Minister has consistently refused to state on what basis equalization payments would be made, we know that Mr. Frost is on record as being opposed to the present basis of payment.

I should now like to deal with the attitude of the premier of the province of Quebec. I hope that my friends who made so many noises down at the other end of the chamber last evening when some of my colleagues were speaking will feel that I am not dealing with this subject in any personal manner whatsoever. I regard the premier of the province of Quebec as a friend. I had many contacts with the premier of the province of Quebec during the time that I was president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority and all of the relationships were on a high level; all of them were cordial. I should not like anything that I have to say here to be taken as a reflection upon the premier of Quebec.
But facts are facts. The facts are there. The record can be seen by any one. That is why I should like to deal for a moment with the attitude of the premier of the province of Quebec.

As we all know, Mr. Duplessis has never committed himself to any concrete proposal on the matter of fiscal arrangements. When he presented a bill in 1954 to levy a provincial income tax, he included in the bill a preamble stating that the provinces had a prior right to direct taxes over that of the federal government, as the hon. member for Bellechasse sought to establish a moment ago in his able discourse. But eventually Mr. Duplessis withdrew from that position and that statement contained in the preamble of the bill was dropped altogether. When he came to the conference in Ottawa held in October of 1955, he failed to make any concrete proposals.

Here are the conclusions that were listed in the brief presented by the province of Quebec and read by the premier of that province to the conference. The conclusions were three in number and I list them. They are to be found at page 40 of the report of the dominion-provincial conference, 1955:

column2: Clarification and delimitation of the powers of taxation of both the federal and provincial authorities, in accordance with the letter and spirit of the Canadian constitution, that is to say having regard to the past, the present and the future.
Simplification of public taxation in such a way as to reduce its cost and facilitate its collection.
Moderation in the domain of taxation to be arrived at by the collaboration of all public powers, in such a way as to ease the burden of the taxpayer so far as possible.

column1: I am sure that anybody in this house who has given any thought to the matter-and I hope that includes the hon. member for Bellechasse-will agree with me when I say that there is certainly no concrete proposal in those three conclusions but rather a great deal of vagueness and confusion. As hon. members will recall, between 1955 and 1957 the system of fiscal arrangements with the provinces was completely changed by the then Liberal federal administration. With regard to the changes made Mr. Duplessis has said that they were a step in the right direction.

However, two years later, in November of 1957, Mr. Duplessis came to Ottawa and presented to the conference-that is the one which was held last fall-the very same brief, word for word, that he had presented in 1955. I have both of them here in my hand. I invite hon. members of the house to read the briefs. I have gone over them carefully. I say here in the house that the brief presented by the premier of the province of
Quebec in 1955 and the one presented in 1957 are the same, word for word.

So that there may be no ambiguity about it, I now read from page 28 of the report of the federal-provincial conference proceedings of 1957. Here are the conclusions of the brief presented by the premier of the province of Quebec:

column2: Clarification and delimitation of the powers of taxation of both the federal and provincial authorities, in accordance with the letter and spirit of the Canadian constitution, that is to say having regard to the past, the present and the future.
Simplification of public taxation in such a way as to reduce its cost and facilitate its collection.
Moderation in the domain of taxation to be arrived at by the collaboration of all public powers, in such a way as to ease the burden of the taxpayer so far as possible.

column1: I could go on and read paragraph after paragraph to indicate to the house that the two briefs were exactly the same.

So here again, in so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, there is complete vagueness and confusion. As I asked earlier, what is the position of the government with reference to these equalization payments? Here are four different approaches to the problem of federal-provincial relations and I therefore ask the government and particularly the Quebec members to define their attitudes with respect to these four positions I have just described. Are they in favour of the government proposal? Are they in favour of Mr. Frost's formula? Do they want to see equalization payments lowered as was suggested by Mr. Frost? 1940584,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.22.41,1958-06-03,8db7e861-18f0-4588-865a-0bb29f90f20b,ca.m.3390,Mr. G. W. Montgomery (Victoria-Carleton):,,DOMINION-PROVINCIAL FISCAL RELATIONS,,,Mr. Speaker, having sat in this house for the short period of about five and a half years-very memorable years for that part of the country from which I come-I feel I should say something on this motion. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said in his opening remarks that the debate would give new members from Quebec, Ontario and other provinces an opportunity to speak on this problem, that is to say, the problem of federal-provincial relations. I should like to compliment the hon. Leader of the Opposition on having introducing the amendment he did, because I believe it is one of the best amendments which the opposition has put forward. It is a lot better than some which have preceded it, but I suppose they will improve as time goes by, and we should expect that.

I think this amendment has opened up an important debate, a debate which, by the time it is over, will result, I am satisfied, in hon. members of the opposition and the people in the country generally being a lot wiser than they were before it started. Unless the opposition can convince this house and the country that the arguments they are using are sound there can, however, be nothing constructive about the amendment which they have introduced. So far I have listened to all the arguments used, and some of them are good. For once, I should like to compliment the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) who has just preceded me. I think I have listened to one of his finest speeches.

But I should like to deal first of all with the remarks made by the hon. Leader of the Opposition. In introducing his amendment yesterday he stressed one point beyond all others, using all his efforts to try to lead this house and the country into believing that the Conservative party under our present Prime Minister and government had repudiated the principle of equalization. I could not help thinking while he was speaking that he was only building up a straw man in order to knock it down. I think the best way I can answer him would be by repeating the reply given to him last September when he stressed that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) while in opposition had promised to call a dominion-provincial conference. Nobody has ever disputed that. But no government in the history of parliament had ever taken over such a mess as the present Prime Minister and his government did in June, 1957.

I should like to point out that it is impossible to organize a conference overnight, and in support of my statement I should like to refer to the conference which was arranged in October of 1955. How long did it take the

former government to organize a federal-provincial conference on that occasion? Over a year. These things cannot be done overnight. The Conservative government did call a conference and in his opening remarks at that conference the Prime Minister had these words to say:

I think at the very beginning you have a right and you are entitled to a statement as to the general attitude to be taken by the new government. We desire to achieve harmony in the operation of our governmental institutions in Canada. We respect the constitution and we fully recognize the constitutional responsibilities of the provinces.

The Prime Minister went on to say that while in opposition his party had criticized not the principle but the extent to which the federal treasury should contribute to the funds of provincial governments and, later, commenting on fiscal relations, he said there were special problems facing the Atlantic provinces. He refrained from saying anything about those problems in connection with Newfoundland because at that time a royal commission was sitting in compliance with the terms of federation, with a view to making recommendations as to what Newfoundland should receive. But the Prime Minister did refer to the maritime provinces, and he said-and this was apparently agreed to by all the provinces:

I believe we all recognize that the Atlantic provinces as a group are confronted with greater difficulties in public finance than the rest of the nation, if they are to maintain the sort of provincial and municipal services that Canadians generally expect. The taxable capacity of the Atlantic provinces, even in the best of times, is significantly lower than that of the other provinces.

It must be frankly admitted that to a degree this disparity has been overcome by the equalization payments under the tax sharing arrangements. The government of New Brunswick argued at the last conference that for the Atlantic provinces the disparity of taxable capacity is so great that this equalization in respect of the major direct tax fields is not enough.

The Prime Minister was referring, of course, to the three fields of taxation as defined under the principle of equalization as laid down by the former government, namely the fields of income tax, sales tax and succession duties. He concluded, and this is a summary of his remarks and I think the meaning is very plain:

We wish to review the tax sharing arrangements themselves. I believe that the dominion treasury should help to equalize and stabilize provincial revenues. Recognizing these principles, we are prepared to examine their application and to that end I invite the expression of your views.
There is the answer to the Leader of the Opposition, and it was given last November when that conference was held. It is there for all who have eyes to read or ears to hear.
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations

The Leader of the Opposition laboured very hard to try to convince hon. members of this house and, particularly, I imagine, the considerable number of new members, that this principle of equalization was something new, that it was a miracle, that it was something discovered by the Liberal party which was going to cure all the ills of Canada. And having listened to the speeches made in this debate I think there are even now hon. members on the opposition side of the house who still believe that equalization will cure all the country's ills.

I have heard speeches made both inside and outside of this house over the last four and one half or five years on the question of federal-provincial relations. I do not think any one party or any government can take credit for devising the principle of equalization. It is true that it was spoken of by the former prime minister. It was pointed out as desirable by the former premier of Nova Scotia and talked about by the present premier of that province. It was put forward in a different way by the premier of New Brunswick at various conventions and conferences. It was arrived at finally out of the whole consideration. I cannot understand how any hon. gentleman opposite could stand up in this house before we who have been here previously and who know the history of it and have the audacity to try to make us believe that the former government devised, found and discovered this miracle and wants to adhere to it. No one is condemning the principle of equalization which is good as far as it goes.

There is one thing about the present government which I admire. While it has adopted this principle it has not made it final. It still has an open mind and is ready to hear the provinces on the subject and if improvements can be made they will be made. That is a sound approach to the question.

I am going to refer to certain statements made at the federal-provincial conference held in Ottawa on October 3, 1955 and then I shall attempt to draw comparisons between the former government and its actions in relation to its words, and the present government and its actions in relation to what it has said. At page 15 of the proceedings of that conference in the opening statement by Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent, the then prime minister, we find this statement:

-the present government had no Intention of abandoning the objective of the tax rental agreements which is to make it financially possible for all the provinces, whatever their tax base, to perform their constitutional functions themselves and to provide a reasonable Canadian level of provincial services without an abnormal burden of taxation. That is the foundation of the policy of the federal government.
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations
On that occasion Mr. St. Laurent was restating words he had used in writing to the premiers of the provinces in January 1955. The hon. gentleman went on to say:
This is the principle of paying an element of fiscal need subsidies to provinces with lesser tax potential than others.
That was carried through but Premier Hicks of Nova Scotia as reported at page 43 of that report indicated how it fell short when he said:

It is now evident that the relative capacity of the different provinces to provide even a minimum standard of services cannot be determined by reference to population figures alone ... I suggest that any formula which might be devised should take into consideration not only the population of the province but also its tax potential.

That is the foundation on which the maritime provinces have based their case from the beginning up until they met with the provincial governments last November. Premier Flemming of New Brunswick, as reported at page 50 of the proceedings of the 1955 conference, said:

However, experience has indicated that the tax rental agreements do not go far enough to meet the needs of low income provinces . . . We are firmly convinced that these provinces should receive a national adjustment grant to compensate them for their lack of taxable capacity in respect of those sources of revenue remaining to them.

While I do not intend to read it into the record any hon. member who wishes to examine it can find on that page of the report authority for what I have said in a quotation taken from the Rowell-Sirois commission report, chapter V, book II.

What happened at the 1955 conference? I cannot speak for every premier who attended but I feel that I can speak for the premiers of the Atlantic provinces who according to the general reports carried in the press did not accept that formula of equalization as being sufficient in itself. They did not accept it because it did not give to the maritime provinces sufficient money to provide the services which they ordinarily ought to provide their people to place them on the same standard that obtains in the other provinces. In my own province, for instance, it costs one-third more than the national average per capita to provide young people with an education and I presume a similar ratio applies throughout the Atlantic provinces. We do not have sufficient taxable capacity to make up the difference between equalization payments based on the formula of Mr. Harris, the former minister of finance, and the national average that obtains across the country. That is what we asked for but our request was not recognized.
Early in March 1956 when the premiers met with the minister of finance of the former

government to finalize the result of the conference of October 1955, Mr. Harris said in effect that the proposals offered-meaning the equalization payments-""go just as far as we can go at this time"" and if any province needed more revenue it should go into double taxation levying tolls beyond the federal deductions allowed. In effect he said, ""We cannot at this time make any further material concessions that would adversely affect our revenues"". That was the final statement from the last federal-provincial conference held by the former government.

We had a change of government between then and the federal-provincial conference of November 1957. The premiers of the Atlantic provinces attended the latter conference just as determined as they were when they attended previous ones. They laid their case before the new government. I have described what happened under the previous government. Hon. gentlemen opposite today adhere to the policy that was followed then and if they were in power that is the limit to which they would go. I am satisfied with that on the basis of the speeches I have heard today.

What did the present government do? They realized what the situation was like in the maritime provinces; they immediately took action. The premiers went home feeling much better than they did the year before. Not only that, but they took further action. They have made provision for $100 million to be distributed over the next four years among those four provinces as an adjustment grant to bring up the level to some extent and to meet the request in a temporary manner to some extent until it is finally settled what action should be taken on the requests of those premiers. It is an attitude of give and take; it is an attitude of tolerance which this government has shown and which the old government never was able to show or would not show to the maritimes, which has made our people down east feel that this government is sincere.
While the federal-provincial conference which was adjourned last fall has not been called together it is true that you do not hear any call for it from the premiers.

1940607,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.22.64,1958-06-03,9fa12394-384b-4e7a-872b-8230b0e27dd7,ca.m.3489,Mr. Winch:,,DOMINION-PROVINCIAL FISCAL RELATIONS,,,You are correct, sir. Speaker? You do not, either, want to hear a Pickersgillian policy of profusion and confusion from the opposition.

This is an excellent amendment. It mentions in particular the need for a federal-provincial conference to discuss joint problems of common concern to the federal and provincial authorities. When you mention the provincial authorities it automatically follows that you take in the problems of local governments because local governments are the children of the provincial authorities. These local governments cannot deal directly with the federal government. This fact was admitted recently by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he informed this house it was his intention to hold an informal conference with the representatives of the municipalities sometime in September. There can be no conference on a dominion-provincial basis which does not bring in the problems of the municipalities.

I think that we all have to recognize that greatly changed times and conditions have brought to provincial governments new problems that were not visualized some 100 or more years ago when our local governmental system was formed. New needs have steadily arisen and the task of meeting those needs has, to a great extent, been shouldered by the local authorities. I am convinced that our provincial governments have recognized the requirements of the local governments but have not been in a position to take care of them because of neglect at the federal level. I believe that past and present governments, at the federal level have, thus far, failed to work out policies which would enable provincial and municipal governments to fully discharge their modern responsibilities.

Therefore in the view of our group it is absolutely imperative that a further and early conference be reconvened as soon as possible and that at this conference there shall be recognition on the part of the present government of the need to relate federal responsibilities to the development, protection, conservation and regeneration of the natural resources of this country.

Our friend the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton did not think that provincial premiers were greatly interested in such a matter. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that as recently as this year, in his presentation in the British Columbia legislature of the budget which he introduced as minister of finance, the premier of British Columbia made it clear that British Columbia was most anxious for a further dominion-provincial conference to deal with such problems as all-weather access roads; as well as basic communication or

Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations transport means essential to the economic development of a province; the protection and regeneration of forests; irrigation and reclamation, diking, draining and clearing of agricultural lands; the expansion and development of fisheries and mining operations; and -something that is of importance at the present time-to ask for further federal assistance, in action and in finances, in connection with the applied and pure sciences in the fields of industry. That is something that is most necessary when, as a trading nation- particularly as far as British Columbia is concerned as a trading province-we are losing out on foreign markets.

1 know that as far as British Columbia is concerned, the government feels it is absolutely essential that as soon as possible there shall be an early reconvening of a dominion-provincial conference. Tied in with the items that I have already mentioned there is also necessity of the presentation by the provinces of representations relating to the need for low interest credit facilities both to the provincial and local governments where the growth of basic services and the essential need for them is a result of general economic development.

Just a little while ago I said that we spent too much time in going back into the past, and that it was wrong. But just on one item alone I should like to refer to the past. I do so because it is something which, in my estimation, should be the subject of early consideration at a dominion-provincial conference. I refer to the question of expansion of access roads and railroads. We have heard a great deal about the vision of the Prime Minister and the building of railroads to the north. In the past few years we have not only heard a great deal but we have voted a great deal of money in this House of Commons for the construction of railroads. However, British Columbia has been discriminated against or, shall I say, has been almost left out of the picture. Back on June 3 of 1955 there was introduced into this House of Commons by the then prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, a bill for the provision of a subsidy on a portion of the extension of Pacific Great Eastern Railway in British Columbia. Speaking on that bill the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green)-and I quote from page 4390 of Hansard, volume IV, 1955
had this to say:

Mr. Speaker, the government seems to be in the railway business overnight. I would ask the Prime Minister whether he has given consideration to the speech on this subject made by the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) at the time a subsidy was granted for the extension of the line from Quesnel to Prince George. If he has not done so, I would commend that speech to him.

If he agrees with it I think the government would grant a subsidy for the whole extension into the Peace river area.

That was the statement made by the present Minister of Public Works. It is something which I maintain is of vital interest, at least as far as the province of British Columbia is concerned, for presentation to an early dominion-provincial conference. You can understand the basis for that statement, Mr. Speaker, when I inform this house that since 1953 the province of British Columbia has spent $17J million constructing the P.G.E. from Quesnel to Prince George, $14 million from North Vancouver to Squamish and $54 million from Prince George to the Peace river area. The original cost from Squamish to Quesnel was $27 million. According to my information- and I understand it is factual-the grants made or promised by the federal government for this railway were $2,480,000 or 2.21 per cent of the capital cost of $112,200,000. Having made this expenditure, British Columbia is requesting a total of $19,762,500 or 17.61 per cent of the total original cost. In view of the statement made by one who is now a cabinet minister and in view of the fact that this government has not taken any action to increase the grants to the province of British Columbia with regard to railway construction, this is certainly a matter that we think requires early consideration and we believe it can perhaps be most effectively done at a dominion-provincial conference.

There is one other matter I wish to mention and it is something which is of vital concern, I think, to all municipalities. I refer to the matter of educational costs. It is not something that should be left to an informal conference between municipalities and the cabinet sometime in September. As I said before, the municipalities are the children of a provincial government. They receive grants from a provincial government. Basically and constitutionally I think it is obvious that if it is going to be a straight educational grant it will have to come from the federal government and go through the provincial authority. Therefore, because of the situation in all municipalities on this matter, an early meeting of a dominion-provincial conference is in order, even if it is to be only on the question of educational costs.

The last matter I wish to raise is one of great importance, and that is the problem of obtaining capital financing for the expansion of essential local services in the various cities, towns and municipalities of our country. I want to cite very briefly why these equalization payments are so important. They are important to every province of course, except the province of Ontario which by the nature of things merely receives the value of the taxes; but in all the other provinces the equalization feature is of greater or less

importance depending on the taxable capacity of that province. As I happen to represent one of the provinces with the lowest taxable capacity, it is understandable that I would emphasize that importance perhaps more than some other hon. members in this chamber.

I would like to remind the house what the situation was before we had equalization payments in the Atlantic provinces, or rather in the maritime provinces because Newfoundland was not part of Canada at that time. As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out, at the end of the war, the wartime tax rental agreements were in existence. They were strictly tax rental agreements containing no element of equalization whatever. They simply represented what the provinces had been getting when they gave up temporarily their right to impose the taxes themselves. The three maritime provinces received $7f million. In 1956-57, the last year of the second round of tax rental agreements, the maritime provinces received $43 million. That did not include Newfoundland, of course. In 1957-58 under the equalization formula they received $52 million. Of that sum $32J million was in equalization. The compensation for the taxes was less than $20 million. That represents a sum very nearly twice these very welcome Atlantic provinces grants to those three provinces that were initiated at the instance of this government this year and for which I have always given the government full credit. But I would like to point out that this is precisely what the Minister of Finance said yesterday was zero. He said, ""What did the Liberals do for the maritime provinces? Zero.""

It was done by this parliament of course but I will explain what our Liberal policy accomplished. Incidentally, I might say to the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton that if he can show me anywhere any suggestion of the present principle of equalization before it was announced in this house by Mr. St. Laurent I would be very interested in seeing it. But I do not want to be diverted from my point. What the Minister of Finance said yesterday was that this $32,750,000 to the three maritime provinces in equalization was zero.

If the Atlantic grants, which for those provinces amount to $17,500,000, are a good thing-and they are-surely $32,750,000 is a better thing, and it is. It is more important because it is more permanent; it is based on a definite formula and it is based on a notion which has been accepted by all the provinces as a matter of equity.
What about Newfoundland? In 1957-58 Newfoundland received $17,750,000, of which $12,750,000 is equalization. That is why it

does seem to me that, if anything, the Leader of the Opposition was not speaking quite strongly enough yesterday when he said that we needed, and we need now urgently, to be told what the government's policy really is about equalization, whether the government really intends to maintain the present equalization. It is just not good enough to have the Prime Minister go to Winnipeg and in a speech say he is in favour of equalization because, as the Leader of the Opposition said yesterday-I am not quoting his exact words but I think I am giving the correct sense-it is not only the principle that is important, it is the application of the principle that is important. We want to know, the country wants to know, and certainly those of us who represent the provinces that depend for the maintenance of their most essential services upon those equalization payments, want to know whether this government intends to maintain equalization on the basis of the two provinces with the highest taxable capacity, or whether they have some secret deal with the premier of Ontario that is going to be unveiled after the Manitoba election on June 16 but before July 1, about which we are to be told nothing in the meantime. 1940651,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.23.1.1,1958-06-03,ba1f4916-0b63-4654-9f27-242c3d276e6e,ca.m.6904,Mr. Frank Howard (Skeena):,,TELEVISION,REQUESTS FOR EXTENDED COVERAGE,,Before we proceed to vote on the main motion, there is what might be considered a problem in my area which I should like to draw to the attention of the house. It is one of real importance to those who live in my constituency and, I am sure, it is also of importance to those who live in other out of the way or rural constituencies.

We have for some time been attempting to get a service of television into these more remote areas, but so far we have run against a blank wall, or encountered incomplete answers from those authorities who control television in Canada. I am thinking particularly of one area in my constituency, a well populated area along the coast where approximately 35,000 people live in three communities within a 100 mile radius. We understand that because of certain technological changes and advances which have been made in the field of electronics, and television there can be established at a relatively low cost something akin to a booster station or low frequency relay station, as is used for radio, which would make television in this area possible, but for some odd reason the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is unable or unwilling to take advantage of this development and use it in order to bring television programs to the less populated areas. The answer we have been given, if it is an answer, is that because neither the present government nor the government which preceded it have dealt adequately or publicly with the report of the Fowler commission, the C.B.C. finds itself up against a blank wall with regard to acquiring the necessary equipment for this purpose, or leasing it outright so that those of us who live in less populated parts of the nation may be provided the same sort of entertainment as others who live in the urban areas.

I hope that having raised the question publicly in this way the minister who has jurisdiction over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will undertake to apprise the corporation of the great need which exists for expansion in this direction.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Frank Howard,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ba1f4916-0b63-4654-9f27-242c3d276e6e&Language=E&Section=ALL
1940652,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.23.1.2,1958-06-03,b815a117-7953-4900-b152-afc56dfc44a1,ca.m.5560,Mr. H. W. Herridge (Kootenay West):,,TELEVISION,REQUESTS FOR EXTENDED COVERAGE,,Mr. Speaker, I will not detain the house for more than a moment, but I do wish to bring to the attention of the minister a problem arising in connection with the development of television in local areas where it is not provided at the present time by the C.B.C. In my constituency a number of community groups have got together and are prepared to operate a television service at their own cost on a non-profit basis, and yet under the present regulations these persons are denied a licence. I think this is most unwarranted, because in denying a licence to these people you are denying to the people of that area the opportunity to enjoy a certain amount of television that they are willing to provide at their own expense.
The second point I wish to mention is this: a licence is required for the installation of what is known as piped-in television in cities such as Nelson, and these licences are

apparently approved by the department of the federal government which issues them, but there does not seem to be any control over the charges made for installation or disconnection. I have received numerous complaints about over-charging in these respects, and I have taken them up with the appropriate department of the federal government, only to find that the federal government has no jurisdiction over the rates and charges made for connecting and disconnecting. At the same time, there is no control vested in the public utilities commission of British Columbia. I realize that this development has in recent years been of great magnitude, but I do suggest that this matter be given consideration in order that these charges may be controlled at either provincial or federal level.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Herbert Wilfred Herridge,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b815a117-7953-4900-b152-afc56dfc44a1&Language=E&Section=ALL

Fisher (Port Arthur):,,TELEVISION,REQUESTS FOR EXTENDED COVERAGE,,Mr. Speaker, speaking to this grievance is something like flogging a dead horse. At least, last session we beat the horse rather hard. Reading a good many western newspapers, I have been delighted to note that a number of Conservative members elected to this parliament have also gone on record as being in favour of establishing C.B.C. television stations in remote areas of the hinterland.

As the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) has pointed out the costs are not as great as were originally anticipated. One of the factors which in my opinion has not been made perfectly clear is that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has made exhaustive engineering studies of the prospect. I believe they have on paper a provisional setup for relatively complete television coverage in the remote areas. It seems a pity, as was also pointed out by the hon. member for Skeena, that the delay on the part of the government in implementing the recommendations of the Fowler commission has kept them from going ahead and has contributed to the bitterness of the people in the hinterland over their failure to receive television.

One result caused by the slowness of the government in implementing those recommendations has been that a number of communities have engaged in costly experiments in installing their own aerials and receiving systems. For example, I could name two small communities in my own constituency which spent over $10,000 in developing antennae and which found after all that expense that television reception is still poor. One of the sad aspects of the particular cases in question is that these communities were not able to receive advice from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as to where stations are likely to be located. It was interesting to 57071-3-52
Television Coverage

note that last fall the only inkling we had as to where Canadian Broadcasting Corporation receiving stations would be located in northern Ontario leaked out through the Bell Telephone Company which was informed of the arrangements because of its microwave relay setup.

At the present time our hinterland communities are disappointed, not only in that they do not receive television reception, but also they are keenly disappointed about the radio reception they get from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. In some instances they have no reception at all and in other places they have repeater stations which carry trans-Canada network programs. If any hon. gentlemen listen regularly to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation they will know that the diet carried on the trans-Canada network is pretty heavy in relation to the diet carried on the dominion network. During the election campaign I had the pleasure while motoring one Wednesday evening of hearing for half an hour the voice of a professor who was able to put me to sleep, lecture after lecture, while I was at university. For half an hour his readings went out over the airwaves into a community where I would doubt if poetry as such is read any day of the year by any one in the community.

However, when it comes to radio and television services, we feel that we are being discriminated against.

own radio station. I believe they completely satisfied the governing board of the C.B.C. that the organization, the Burnaby Broadcasting Company, has adequate financial resources. We believe there is discrimination in other matters as well as in radio and television. I might list those other instances; however, this is not the time to go into other fields.

I understand that the application has not yet been refused. Yet, we do find that on every occasion in the past when an applica-toin has been made for the allocation of certain frequencies, the older, the well established and very often the politically reinforced existing radio stations have been able to get the preference and our man has had to return home and report to the business and commercial concerns that over the years have actively supported him that once again he has been denied. Having spoken of radio I also wish to say a few words about television services. The only other programs I can see-and I can see a number of other programs-are United States programs, and those United States programs are in the main being paid for by Canadian advertising, or a goodly number of them.
