Hardie (Mackenzie River):,,BROADCASTING,REQUESTS FOR EXTENSION OF SERVICES,,Mr. Speaker, while many millions of people in Canada are enjoying facilities provided by television at the present time, in the isolated territories of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon we not only do not have the facilities or have the opportunity to enjoy television, we have not proper radio coverage or radio reception. As a matter of fact, in a good many places in the north in order to hear radio the people have to tune into Moscow or other Russian stations, Moscow Molly or newscasts from Russia. As was stated by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories and also by the commissioner of the Yukon territories when they presented their brief to the Fowler commission some time ago, there is a danger of selling Russian ideologies to the people in the isolated areas of our northland.

I admit that the providing of radio reception to the Northwest Territories is a difficult and costly proposition. Atmospheric conditions in that part of the country are such, as I understand from engineers of the C.B.C., that a radio transmitter set up in Texas, or in some other place in the southern parts of the United States of America, would have a better chance of reaching us than radio stations in the populated parts of Canada. That is because of the atmospheric conditions in the northern hemisphere. But the Fowler commission did suggest in their report that aside from the expenditures of the C.B.C., the federal government should provide moneys to build transmitters in Winnipeg and in Vancouver to boom into both the eastern and western Arctic.

I would hope, that at this session or in this year's estimates the government would provide sums of money to begin the immediate construction of those transmitters in order to give the people of the northern regions some communications with the outside world.
Radio Broadcasting-Northern Areas

,Liberal,,Mervyn Arthur Hardie,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=e9692202-913c-4e37-a7ea-4ae0a612ed6e&Language=E&Section=ALL

Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):,Minister of National Revenue,BROADCASTING,REQUESTS FOR EXTENSION OF SERVICES,,Mr. Speaker, in view of the widespread interest in this matter perhaps I should say a word or two before the motion is put. First, may I say to the hon. member for Mackenzie River (Mr. Hardie), that if he has looked at his supplementary estimates, as I am sure he has, he will find there a substantial vote for the installation of this radio system about which he has been speaking. I quite realize that the Fowler commission recommended the installation of a shortwave service from Winnipeg and Vancouver to cover all of that area which the hon. gentleman represents, and a wider area as well.

Although we have not followed completely the recommendation of the Fowler commission in that respect, we have accepted the recommendation of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and we have included in the supplementary estimates a substantial amount of money for the immediate installation of radio services for that area which, heretofore, has been served in part, and to the very best of their ability, by a number of smaller stations, most of which require new equipment and are not in a financial position to continue. I believe, therefore, in that respect at any rate, in so far as that grievance of the hon. member is concerned, I am happy to say that I think we are meeting it, perhaps not 100 per cent but at least to a degree which I am sure he will find satisfactory.

This installation is experimental in nature. As the hon. member points out, atmospheric difficulties are such that even with two transmitters at each station it is possible that atmospheric conditions will be such that reception will be impossible either from Winnipeg or from Vancouver with both transmitters operating. We are starting with one at the moment in an attempt to work out a solution and see what may be the answer in meeting the technical requirements. After the station has been set up for a year or two we may know more about the problem.

In so far as the general problem is concerned, there is no doubt that everyone in Canada wants better radio and television services. I have every sympathy and every appreciation for those who are living in areas which today are not too well served by the existing facilities. There has been some suggestion here that the C.B.C. has failed to do something, has neglected to do something or has refused to do something; that is simply arrant nonsense. The C.B.C. has not failed or refused to do anything. The C.B.C. has been spending the money which
this parliament has made available to it, and spending it to the very best effect possible.

In that connection I should like to point this out. This year, under the aegis of this government-I am not speaking politically now at all because other governments gave the C.B.C. financial support, too-

,Liberal,,George James McIlraith,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=20afcc72-88d0-433e-8b61-a7bcd98b2ec9&Language=E&Section=ALL
1940675,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.24.1.4,1958-06-03,ea30e79d-1feb-461a-bbea-b3e5a570ee30,ca.m.468,Mr. Nowlan:,Minister of National Revenue,BROADCASTING,REQUESTS FOR EXTENSION OF SERVICES,,You did a good job with it; there is no question about that, but we are going to do a better one with it. As a matter of fact, without transgressing or getting involved in a political discussion, I should just point out that the former government provided enough money to operate the C.B.C. up until last October. I presume this was because the Fowler commission had been set up, because the government was awaiting the report of that commission and because the government expected, in the peace and serenity of their minds and souls which still dominated them even a year ago tonight, that they would have an opportunity to scan the Fowler commission report and bring in supplementary estimates last fall. In any event, when we came into office we faced a situation in which the C.B.C. would have ground to a full stop last October because their estimates were exhausted. As I have said, I presume that was because the former government expected the Fowler commission report to be brought in and they hoped, expected and assumed that they would be introducing an appropriation to enable the C.B.C. to continue. As we know, something happened. They had the peace, serenity and time to consider the report, but they did not have much to do with implementing it or bringing in a vote.

As a result, the first thing that had to be done last fall was the provision of a vote to enable the C.B.C. to carry on for the balance of the year. This, we did. We introduced a vote in this house, as recommended by the Fowler commission, for the first annual instalment. We provided half of it. I have not the figures in front of me for this year. Frankly, I did not expect this question would come up or I should have been prepared. I have not my documents here; they are all down in the other office. However, speaking in general terms, we have provided several million dollars more this year than has ever been provided before for the C.B.C. The service is being expanded as rapidly as possible. As some hon. members know who have been listening to the debate on the address, there has been criticism of the government for having made too much money available to the C.B.C. I do not subscribe to that criticism for one moment.

In that connection, too, it should be pointed out that the figures are somewhat misleading because at the suggestion-it was either of the preceding government, the Fowler commission or both, but it was a proper suggestion-the C.B.C. divested itself of many of the investments it had held up until last year. During the days of the 15 per cent excise tax, the revenue from which was credited to the C.B.C., the C.B.C. invested in certain securities. I believe the giving of this tax money to the C.B.C. was a mistake, because the revenue bore no relationship whatever to the needs of the C.B.C. When everybody was buying television sets, millions of dollars rolled into the C.B.C., whether or not they needed the money. When the people stopped buying television sets, the C.B.C. needed still more money which it could not get from the excise tax and therefore had to hope that the treasury of Canada, the consolidated revenue fund, would make up the difference.

In any event, during those lush days when the 15 per cent excise tax was piling up a surplus for the C.B.C., it did invest millions of dollars in Dominion of Canada bonds and other securities which last year it sold. When one looks at the parliamentary vote of a year ago and looks at the parliamentary vote today, therefore, I do not want any hon. member assuming we have made an additional $17 million or $18 million available. You have to deduct from our vote the surplus assets, the securities which were sold last year.

As I have said, I have every sympathy with those areas that require better service. There is no area in Canada which does not require or ask for better service, whether it is an isolated area or whether it is a centre of population. The C.B.C. is doing its best to meet these demands. I would point out to the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), who talked about the Fowler commission and what it recommended, that the Fowler commission did not recommend any instantaneous transformation of the situation which exists today. It would not follow, therefore, that one moment my friend would be lulled to sleep by the drowsy voice of that college professor who put him to sleep 10 or 15 or 20 years ago, and the next day we would have created new facilities entirely. The Fowler commission envisaged that this perhaps would be done over a period of five to ten years. It is impossible to do it earlier because the cost is tremendous. Today, over 80 per cent of the people of Canada are being served by television, and a somewhat larger percentage are being served by radio. Even the Fowler commission said that 10 per cent of the population could never be served, either by television or radio, because the cost
Radio Broadcasting-Northern Areas would be so great that no government could vote the money and expect public support.

I am not saying this is going to be the policy of this government, but when my friend talks about what the Fowler commission said, and what we should do, I think he should stick more closely to the text of the Fowler commission and perhaps not be lulled to sleep by the college professor when he was driving along the road.

There has been a great deal said about competition, and I think this should be put on the record for the benefit of the C.B.C. In the United States of America, that great nation to the south of us, 55 per cent of the area, not of the population but 55 per cent of the area of the United States, has available to it only one television station. In other words, these areas have no competing stations. This statement, of course, does not apply to Chicago, New York or Boston, but over 55 per cent of the entire area of the United States has available to it only one television station, if any.

1940677,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.24.1.6,1958-06-03,ea30e79d-1feb-461a-bbea-b3e5a570ee30,ca.m.468,Mr. Nowlan:,Minister of National Revenue,BROADCASTING,REQUESTS FOR EXTENSION OF SERVICES,,That may be. I pay tribute

where tribute is due. I think that the Liberal government deserves a tribute once in a while for some of the things it did, at any rate. I want to point out this fact also. In the United States of America there are three television networks and according to the financial reports none of them, as networks, are making much money, if they are breaking even. The United States has a population of 165 million or 170 million people. We have a population of between 16,500,000 and 17 million. We have a national network for television and we also have a French network for television. In other words, we are maintaining two television networks with a population of 16J million whereas the United States of America is finding great difficulty in maintaining three networks with a population of roughly 170 million. I say therefore that on the whole we are not doing too badly in extending the services under the circumstances which exist today. I think it is generally recognized in so far as our radio is concerned or our radio programs, that the standard and quality of the C.B.C. will compare favourably with any radio network or any radio system in the world.

I would also call this point to the attention of my good friend the hon. member for Port Arthur, who was worrying a while ago about what the Fowler commission says about getting ahead and developing his area and who also wanted to see more light music, shall we say, on the dominion network as contrasted with the trans-Canada network.
Radio Broadcasting-Northern Areas

May I say that if we adopt the Fowler commission report in toto-it suggests that the dominion network could be abolished- and then he will only have the opera of the C.B.C. to listen to and not even the drowsy voice of the college professor.

Anyway, I want to assure the house, and the hon. gentleman who raised this matter in a way which I appreciate, that the government and the C.B.C. are conscious of the responsibility which rests upon them, the government to supply the money and the C.B.C. to supply the service. It is my belief and conviction that the C.B.C. will continue to develop this service and provide even a better one than it has previously. As I said to the hon. member for Mackenzie, we are going to extend in other more or less, shall I say, isolated areas, as rapidly as possible.
I think the service which will be given by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to the people of Canada will be one of which all Canadians can be well and truly proud.

1940712,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.26.8.1.1.1,1958-06-03,,,,stagedirection,,,,The house resumed, from Friday, May 30, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Monteith (Perth)-Mr. Sevigny in the chair:
Hospital Insurance Act

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act to authorize contributions being made as of the first day of July, 1958, to a participating province which has a plan in operation; and to make certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.",,,,

1940713,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.26.8.1.2,1958-06-03,b5f37fd9-d8b5-45d5-969c-c8a112edab19,ca.m.4091,Mr. Bourque:,,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,HOSPITAL INSURANCE ACT,"AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.","Mr. Chairman, when my speech was interrupted last Friday at five o'clock for other business I was saying that when the Conservatives were in opposition they were loud in their condemnation of the policy of the Liberal government in not having allowed the hospitals a substantial amount for depreciation on the building and maintenance costs of hospitals. What has caused them to drop these items from the bill they are now presenting to this house? What has caused the Conservatives now that they are in power to change their minds? Why does the government now feel the Liberals were right in refusing to include these items in the act which they were presenting on the prior occasion? It is paying an indirect tribute to the Liberal government which introduced this legislation; it is an admission by the Conservative government that the Liberal government was fully justified in its refusal to bear the depreciation on the cost of building and maintenance.

It might be interesting to this house to learn from the Minister of National Health and Welfare what progress he has made with the provinces with respect to the hospital insurance act. Has the minister personally discussed this measure with the premiers of the different provinces since this government came to power? If only one province so far seems to be entirely in favour of the act and is ready to join with the federal government in its administration, this surely does not indicate that he has met with much success. The provinces appear to be more anxious to keep aloof than to join with the federal government to put this legislation into effect. The hon. minister told us the other day that five provinces were ready to sign the agreement. Why have they not signed? Why are they delaying if, as the minister says, they are in complete agreement?

Under the Liberal government tuberculosis and mental cases were not included under the act. The reason for this, it was contended, was that the provincial governments collected the taxes for this purpose and that they should therefore bear the cost of such cases. In other words, the then federal government did not feel it should subsidize any provincial government when taxes were collected for a specific purpose, as was the case in respect

Hospital Insurance Act to tuberculosis and mental cases. I understand this applies also in Great Britain where a health insurance plan is in operation. In this instance the Conservatives, who were then in opposition, argued that tuberculosis and mental cases should be covered by the act.

Is the Conservative government willing to admit that once again the Liberal government was right? I would like to call the attention of this house to the fact that they have left such cases out of the bill they are now presenting for approval-another tribute to the Liberal government which first brought the hospital insurance act into being.

Under the Liberal regime six provincial governments had agreed in principle to join the federal government in bringing this act into effect. What has happened to all these provinces? It would now appear that the only province which is in entire accord with the federal government is Ontario, which has no hospital insurance scheme in force and would therefore not be eligible to enter this scheme. It was expected that the legislation would be carried into effect on or about January 1, 1959, and it would appear that the only provinces eligible to take advantage of the act are the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, since they are the only provinces with hospital insurance schemes in effect at this time.

The minister stated that it was now the intention of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Alberta and Newfoundland to begin operations by July. He also stated that Nova Scotia was hoping to commence operations on January 1 next and that Ontario had signed the agreement. Why did the other provinces not sign?

I feel a tribute should be paid to those responsible for the introduction of the hospital insurance act, the then minister of national health and welfare and the then prime minister. I should also mention here the splendid co-operation and support they received from the Conservative premier of the province of Ontario, the Hon. Mr. Frost and, if I may do so, I will compliment the present Minister of Health and Welfare for having again brought this bill before the house. I have no doubt that this measure will ease the minds of many people who have for years lived in fear of sickness or ill health. It is a good step forward, and I hope it will prove a successful one. I believe this is a good measure instituted by the Liberal party, and that it will meet with the approval of all the elements of society-working men, white collar men, and wealthy men-the approval, in short, of every individual in Canada. We on this side of the house hope

that the government will give the most careful consideration to recommendations that may be made for improvements which the opposition may desire to have incorporated into this bill in order that the citizens of Canada may derive from it the greatest possible benefit.

,Liberal,,Romuald Bourque,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b5f37fd9-d8b5-45d5-969c-c8a112edab19&Language=E&Section=ALL
1940714,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.26.8.1.3,1958-06-03,95a5d297-cff6-4bbb-bcf4-8951bad11b91,ca.m.7899,Mr. Granger:,,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,HOSPITAL INSURANCE ACT,AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.","Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks in this debate. The government of Newfoundland, in anticipation of decisions to be reached by this house earlier this year, formulated an extensive program designed to increase hospital accommodation in Newfoundland. Under the program as announced by Premier Smallwood in February of this year, a total of 1,200 beds would be added to hospital accommodation in Newfoundland.

The consideration of the governments concerned, aimed at providing a workable system of federal-provincial hospital insurance, is an example of modern, enlightened, social legislation. I cannot help mentioning that it originated with a previous Liberal government and that it was piloted by the hon. member for Essex East.

Mr. Chairman, I think I should like here to outline the Newfoundland provincial program. The program is to build seven new general hospitals, six new children's hospitals, and to enlarge seven of the existing institutions. The new general hospitals will be as follows: Corner Brook, with 75 beds; Grand Falls, 75 beds; Gander, 80 beds; Cla-renville, 50 beds; Bell Island, 50 beds; Baie Verte Peninsula 30 beds. The projected St. John's mental hospital will have 30 beds. The new children's hospitals will be as follows: Corner Brook, with 40 beds; Grand Falls, 50 beds; Gander, 30 beds; Bell Island, 25 beds; Clarenville, 25 beds; St. John's 200 beds.
The cottage hospitals to be enlarged are as follows: Placentia, Fogo, Brookfield, Bonne Bay, Stephenville Crossing, Bunin and Old Perlican cottage hospital where work has already started.

In addition to these new hospitals, and extensions to existing hospitals, residences will be built for medical doctors at Brookfield, Hermitage, and St. Joseph's. Doctor's residences will be renovated at Burin, St. George's and Stephenville Crossing. Additional medical doctors are to be stationed at Jeffrey's, St. Lawrence, Port Saunders, Old Perlican, Hampden, Stephenville Crossing and Brookfield.

Besides these new hospitals and extensions to hospitals, the government is constructing a new $2 million cancer wing for the general hospital in St. John's. Moreover, the government plans a new 300-bed residence for nursing students at St. John's.

The deliberations of this house regarding a federal-provincial hospital insurance plan will be watched with earnest interest by the many people who will derive real benefit from it and, I might add, a society which allows people to sicken and die for lack of medical treatment belongs to the barbarous past. I am glad the province of Newfoundland is one of the provinces in this co-operative undertaking to provide hospital care for all citizens.

At this time, I would again make another plea on behalf of federal support for the hospital at Gander. Gander is almost wholly a Department of Transport town. At the present time there are always a number of beds held vacant in case of an emergency. It seems to me, and indeed to many others, that the Gander hospital is largely a federal responsibility and I do hope that favourable consideration will be given to this suggestion.
May I ask, with due modesty and faith, that the breadth of the new vision include the much needed facilities for Gander.

,Liberal,,Charles Ronald McKay Granger,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=95a5d297-cff6-4bbb-bcf4-8951bad11b91&Language=E&Section=ALL
1940715,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.26.8.1.4,1958-06-03,ba1f4916-0b63-4654-9f27-242c3d276e6e,ca.m.6904,Mr. Howard:,,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,HOSPITAL INSURANCE ACT,AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.","Mr. Chairman, in the past number of days, not only while the committee has been dealing with this resolution but while the house has been dealing with other matters, we have heard periodically, especially from government backbenchers, the theme that this is a government which keeps its promises. On every possible occasion where they can use that approach, it is used.

Those of us who come from British Columbia and who have some familiarity with the political picture there in the last five or six years can see that there is a definite parallel between this approach-the theme that this is a government which keeps its promises-and the government we have in British Columbia. Quite frankly, I think this is a smart psychological approach-to leave, or create the impression in the minds of the general public that this is a government which keeps faith with the people.

But in order to balance the scale it is necessary to show the other side of the coin, as it were, and point out instances where this government has not kept faith with the people, occasions when it has not kept its own promises. I refer not only to election promises, but to the sort of changes it wanted to make when it was sitting in opposition.

In attempting to strike this balance with regard to only one phase of the business of the committee, that is to say with regard to this resolution, I would merely remind hon. members opposite of three particular promises that were made by this government relating to the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic

Hospital Insurance Act Services Act. One of them relates to patients in tuberculosis sanitaria, another to patients in mental hospitals and the third to reflecting the depreciation cost of hospitals. These matters were not only the subject of election campaign promises; they were the subject matter of speeches which were made by the gentlemen on your right, Mr. Chairman, when they were sitting in opposition. I believe that two of them were the subject matter of the amendment to the original bill which the Liberal government introduced, to the effect that the cost of keeping patients in tuberculosis sanataria and mental hospitals should be reflected in the grant. Thus, we have a three-fold promise, or a promise from three different angles made in speeches, amendments and then in a space of irresponsible election pledges with regard to these matters I have mentioned. We do not, of course, agree with the attitude of the official opposition which coincides at the present time with the attitude they took when they were in government.

I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) at least attempted to leave the impression that he wanted to live up to these promises by spending the provincial governments' money to carry them out because at the federal-provincial conference last fall, in a futile attempt to abandon part of the load of promises, he suggested that if the federal government were to include in the plan the cost of patients in tuberculosis sanatoria and mental hospitals the federal government would have to reduce the amount of general grants which are made to the provinces by the amount it would cost to provide that additional hospital care. It is easy to keep a promise if you are going to spend someone else's money in doing it. In addition to that we had what might be described as the sorry spectacle of the Minister of Finance yesterday saying that no such commitment was made by his government at the federal-provincial conference last November.

While I am sure no hon. member of this committee will vote against this resolution because the slight change it does provide is acceptable, nevertheless it is merely a feeble attempt to move toward what, should be a sensible and all-inclusive health plan for Canada. The people do not want participation by the federal government in hospital insurance coverage but rather they want something akin to the all-inclusive health plan envisaged by the Liberal party in that 40-year old manifesto adopted in 1919. Actually the measure before us is of relatively little value because it makes but a minor change in the operation of the existing act.
As you know, the party to which I belong has spent many years campaigning both

Hospital Insurance Act inside this house and outside of it for an allinclusive national health plan. We have ideas about the scope and institution of such a plan which differ from those conceptions held by the Liberal party and the Conservative government. We merely ask the government, if it will do nothing else, to at least keep faith with the people of this country to whom it made promises by bringing in changes in line with the ideas expressed by hon. members of the government less than a year ago. Naturally we would like to see the government go further. We would like to see the act amended in such a way as to lay the groundwork for an all-inclusive doctor-dental health plan on a national scale but designed in keeping with our constitutional provisions to respect the jurisdiction of the provinces in the field of health.

In a proper national health scheme such as we have advanced over the years there should be emphasis placed on prevention of illness and I will deal with that subject more fully in a moment. At this point I should give the government fair warning that we will continue in our efforts to persuade it to give leadership in instituting the kind of plan we envisage.

Although the numerical representation of the C.C.F. group in this house is not large we hope that in years to come we will be able to bring enough pressure to bear on the government so that it will, as was the case with the Liberal government on so many occasions in years past, come to realize that the ideas we express are necessary and will bring in legislation embodying the principles we advance.

In the operation of the act as it exists at this time there is a failure in that emphasis should first be placed on providing facilities for the determination and correction of illness in its early stages. The measure before us contemplates participating in an insurance program that pays for the individual part of the costs of treatment after he becomes ill enough to enter hospital. If we place the emphasis on prevention we will be taking a forward step in providing for the health and welfare of the Canadian population.

There are health plans in effect in a number of countries of the world. Unfortunately Canada lags far behind many other nations in providing health care, services and insurance coverage for the people who need it. We are not alone in that respect because our good neighbour to the south is in precisely the same position. Let me draw the attention of the committee to some fairly prominent countries that have adopted all-inclusive health plans which go further than the system envisaged in the resolution before us.
Probably the first country in the world to adopt an all-inclusive health scheme was Germany in 1883.

1940717,ca.proc.d.1958-06-03.26.8.1.6,1958-06-03,ba1f4916-0b63-4654-9f27-242c3d276e6e,ca.m.6904,Mr. Howard:,,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,HOSPITAL INSURANCE ACT,AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.","I believe that is correct. I was not alive at that time so I have no personal recollection of it. However, I do recall reading that Bismarck was prominent in Germany at the time this was instituted. I am glad that my friend the hon. member for Essex East, the former minister of national health and welfare, substantiated what I said. It lends me assurance in the points I am attempting to make.

Austria, another European country, was probably the next to adopt a national health plan some five years later in 1888, followed by Hungary in 1891. New Zealand made progressive changes to their existing plan and in 1939 instituted an all-inclusive scheme. I am sure all hon. members are familiar with the plan that is in effect in the United Kingdom which received so much publicity at the time of and following its adoption in 1948. The plan having been adopted in recent years the memory of the newspaper publicity arising out of it is fresh in our minds. Other countries which have had plans in effect for a number of years include Denmark, Norway and The Netherlands. Actually there are 39 other foreign countries that provide for hospital care today for patients when in hospital.

Thirty-eight of those provide medicines. All but one, 38 again, provide for and pay for the services of a specialist. All but two provide for general practitioners' care and treatment of patients. These are countries smaller in area than Canada, some of them less wealthy and smaller in population than Canada or the United States to the south of us; yet many years ago they entered into this all-inclusive doctor-dental care national health schemes, not merely a hospital insurance coverage scheme.

I suppose the history not only of hospital insurance care in Canada but the development of other fields of legislation which were either entirely under the jurisdiction of the provinces or where there was not an overlapping situation but similar jurisdiction in different fields such as in labour has shown that the attitude and the policies of the federal government and the gains of the government generally follow far behind the progress made in the provincial field. An example is the present question that we are discussing.
We have provinces in Canada that have had hospital insurance schemes in effect for a number of years. I do not recall the exact dates of all of them but my own province

has one and I believe it was introduced in 1949, some nine years ago, under a coalition government when incidentally, I should say, a provincial election was around the corner. At that time a provincial hospital insurance scheme was instituted. Before that Saskatchewan, and then Alberta, had a sort of plan. In recent years there has been more thought and more discussion and more ideas presented in other provinces. In addition to that we have been pressing the federal government to institute a national plan even though some of the provinces have their own provincial plans. We finally arrived at the point of following the lead of the provinces in hospital insurance coverage and in finally getting around to participating with them and providing for it.

In our opinion, even if the federal government before last June 10, and this government now, had been desirous-and apparently they were-of confining the federal government's participation to that of taking part in a hospital insurance coverage scheme, they should have taken the lead some years ago and placed the legislation on the statute books. They should have said to the provinces, we will participate with you in covering the costs of a socialized hospital scheme, if you wish to call it that, when you put the plan into effect. When you get it into operation we will show the lead; we will show that we are interested in getting a uniform scheme across Canada and we will participate uniformly in that scheme.

We should have taken that approach some years ago, just as we are now, instead of waiting 10, 12 or 15 years-I do not know how long-or something of that nature until a number of the provinces had entered into an all-inclusive health scheme to provide doctors' care and pay for doctors' bills or dental bills or other preventive measures. Instead of waiting for the provinces to take the lead to institute such plans on their own, instead of waiting until it had become generally popular to follow that lead and participate in those plans, this government should show some leadership in this field by amending the present legislation to share in the

costs of dental care, doctors' care, nursing care and other professional preventive care of ill people, and lay the ground work to participate-in it financially with the provinces to get the plan into effect. We should do that instead of waiting, as we have done in the past, until the provinces show the lead and get the scheme into operation, expand it and come along later and say, that is fine, you have got the schemes under way and we will participate with you in them.
